claims.text: Initially solid FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles are uniformly adsorbed on a three-dimensional porous laser-induced graphene support.
Laser-induced graphene has a high density of defective edge planes.
Defective edge-plane sites immobilize and strongly anchor HEA nanoparticles to laser-induced graphene.
Laser heating produces graphene layers that encapsulate the nanoparticles.
Laser irradiation produces localized thermal hot spots in the FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles.
Localized hot spots cause the constituent metals to melt differentially.
Differences in the constituent metals' melting or decomposition points cause differential melting during irradiation.
Laser conversion of supported mixed-metal precursors can involve thermal decomposition, metal-ion reduction, metal melting, bead fusion, and fission depending on temperature.
Reduced metal species and nanoparticles have limited mobility during solid-phase laser synthesis.
Limited solid-state atomic mobility facilitates the formation of isolated molten domains.
Graphene anchoring and encapsulation stabilize intermediate, partially melted phases.
Graphene anchoring and encapsulation delay complete melting of FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles.
Graphene-supported FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles will have a higher threshold for complete melting than unsupported nanoparticles.
Graphene-supported FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles will exhibit observable intermediate partially molten phases.
Graphene support will slow progression from premelting to full melting and delay morphological and phase evolution.
Unsupported nanoparticles melt earlier and more uniformly because of unmitigated thermal diffusion and higher atomic mobility.
The melting response may vary with laser fluence, precursor concentration, and nanoparticle size distribution.

contradictions.description: The initial material is specified as preformed, initially solid FeNiCrCoCu alloy nanoparticles, but the mechanism invokes thermal decomposition and metal-ion reduction processes characteristic of synthesis from mixed-metal precursors rather than heating of an already metallic alloy nanoparticle.
